figurative

/FIG-yur-uh-tiv/ - the stress falls on FIG · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Figurative means expressing meaning through imagery rather than literal statement.

Nobody at the seed store believed the tomatoes truly drink sunshine, and the clerk's figurative pitch still sold out the flat by noon.

Example

When the news anchor says the river 'shrugged off' the new levee, she speaks in images: rivers have no shoulders, but the borrowed shrug captures what the footage showed — water moving past the barrier as if it were not there. That is figurative speech at work.

Figurative is the umbrella term for meaning carried by imagery instead of literal statement — and it is not a polite word for false. The water really did move past; only the shrug was borrowed. If every element of a whole work carries a second meaning, you have moved past figurative language into allegory.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

metaphorical: Metaphorical names one specific move: speaking through one thing to mean another, as when a deadline 'looms' or a rumor 'spreads like wildfire.' Figurative is the umbrella over that move and its cousins — simile, hyperbole, personification. Every metaphorical phrase is figurative; not every figurative phrase is a metaphor.

symbolic: Symbolic points at objects and images set up to stand for something beyond themselves — a dove for peace, a broken clock for lost time. Figurative describes wording instead: language that trades literal statement for imagery. A symbol sits in the scene; figurative language lives in the phrasing.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

word-for-word: meaning exactly what the words state

matter-of-fact: plain statement with no imagery at all

Where it sits · how far the wording leaves literal reality — vivid → figurative → fantastical

vivid vs. figurative: Vivid is milder than figurative — vivid wording paints sharply but can stay perfectly literal; a vivid fact is still a fact.

fantastical vs. figurative: Fantastical goes further than figurative: figurative language borrows an image while meaning something real, but the fantastical leaves reality behind altogether.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — figur-

Root — figur-: shape, form (Latin figura)

Suffix — -ative

Suffix — -ative: adjective: tending to

Put it together

Put it together: Figur- (shape) + -ative = tending to shape. Latin figura was a thing's form or outline; figurative speech shapes a meaning rather than stating it — the words mold a picture, and the picture carries the point.

Use the root in a new word: disfigure

Use the root in a new word: disfigure: The vandals who disfigured the fountain were caught on the library's cameras by nightfall.

Word Choice

neutral / academic

Figurative is the wide, workhorse label: any wording that trades literal statement for imagery. Reach for it when you need the umbrella; reach for allegory when a whole work sustains the second meaning, and for allusion when the figure points quietly at another work.
